story: Glowing gas in many colours fills the centre of the Omega Nebula, a hotbed of newborn stars cradled in a huge, cold, dark cloud of hydrogen. Also known as M17 and the Swan Nebula, it lies about 5,500 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius. The area in the frame spans about 3,500 times the width of our solar system.

Ultraviolet radiation from young, massive stars just beyond the upper right corner, each about six times the Sun's temperature and 30 times its mass, is evaporating the dense, cold cloud in which they formed. The blistered walls shine with light from excited hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen and sulfur atoms. A rose-like feature to the right of centre glows red from hydrogen and sulfur.

Pockets of dense gas resist the radiation longer than their surroundings, leaving sculpted shapes and isolated islands that may hold developing stars. One island at the centre of the brightest region measures about 10 times the size of our solar system, and a dense feature jutting in from the left edge resembles Orion's Horsehead Nebula.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys combined blue, near-infrared, hydrogen-alpha and doubly ionized oxygen filters. NASA does not publish which colour each filter is assigned.
understand.eye: Some of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and 2.6 hours of exposure gather far more light than an eye can.

explore: The frame covers about 60 percent of the full field the Advanced Camera for Surveys captured. It was among the first pictures from that camera, released shortly after astronauts installed it on Hubble during a servicing mission.
